THE CRITERIA. THE SCREENS. YOUR INPUT.

Kiln Requirements Stages

Kiln carries the requirements half of the Enso Method too, from source material to the phase plan, stopping only where your review is worth the wait.

Today a person runs each requirements stage in a chat of their own, mostly just starting the next one, and Kiln starts only once the phase plan exists.

What we’re building

If any of these is wrong, say so before reading on. The rest of this review is detail within them.

  1. From your source material, Kiln writes the requirements document, refines it, writes and refines the design and writes the phase plan, each stage in a fresh agent session. Source · 2 · 3
  2. Kiln stops for one early review, where a change costs least: right after the requirements document is refined and before any design, and you can turn that wait off. It always stops at a final review before the build, which never starts by itself. Source · 2 · 3 · 4
  3. Nothing else waits for your answer, and you can give feedback at any moment without stopping anything. Source · 2
  4. Kiln runs whatever stages the Enso Method on your computer has, keeping no list of its own, so most method changes need no change to Kiln; an occasional break is fixed in Kiln when it happens. Source · 2 · 3
  5. A home screen lists everything Kiln can work on, from source material to work under way, with where each stands and what it waits for. Source
  6. Work started by hand can be handed to Kiln at any stage, and every stage can still be run by hand; work that already has its phase plan is built as today, with no review added. Source · 2 · 3

Not included

  • Gathering or sorting source material, or cutting it into an initiative of several documents. That stays with you, in your own agent session.
  • Running a whole roadmap, or several pieces of work in one Kiln.
  • A notification when a review is ready.
  • Typing a brief into Kiln, or dropping a folder onto the page.
  • Rewriting Kiln’s tagline and public positioning, revisited once this is built.
  • Changes to the Enso Method. The one Kiln relies on, the method naming where a brief lives, is proposed to the method on its own and lands before this is built. Four others, such as phase planning always writing at least one phase document, are proposed on their own, and nothing here waits for them.

01 / SECTION

The home screen

Run kiln in a repository or a folder of repositories, and a home page lists what Kiln can work on under “Under way”, “Ready to start” and “Not ready yet”, plus a collapsed group at the end for documents Kiln can’t tell are built or unfinished, and a “Not listed?” panel on bringing material in. Source material is what a requirements document is written from: a brief, an intake record of transcripts and documents, or a planned document in an initiative; the shared branch is the one new work is cut from, such as develop.

Key acceptance criteria & mockups

  • Kiln starts only from those three kinds of source material; for any other folder it says which document is missing. Source
  • Source material must be committed on the shared branch before Kiln starts from it; until then Kiln names what to commit. Source · 2
  • Source material leaves the lists once a requirements document or initiative with its folder name exists on any branch, so it isn’t written twice. Source
  • Kiln never reads commit messages to tell built work from unfinished work, since the method may reword them; it uses files, branches and its own records. Source
  • A planned document can be started even when it depends on another not yet in production; its line says the build will have to wait, but Kiln blocks neither. Source
  • Each item opens in a separate Kiln in its own browser tab, and the home screen shows whether each is working, waiting for you, paused or not running. Source
  • From a folder of repositories, it lists the repositories directly inside, not deeper, with a filter for each repository. Source

Assumptions to confirm

HOME-004Confidence: 75%Impact: MediumUnanswered

Should Not ready yet list only material one step from ready, leaving other folders off?

Yes. It lists only material not committed on the shared branch, and intakes started but not finished, whose record isn’t written yet. Each is cleared by one step.

Other folders under source-material/, such as a stakeholder’s reply or a handoff package, are not listed, and the Not listed? panel says so. A handoff dropped in without a brief therefore doesn’t appear.

This departs from the agreed brief, which listed every such folder with its reason.

If you choose otherwise: Listing every such folder, as the brief says, would show 13 lines where this shows 1. Most would be stakeholder replies, each told to add a brief; but a reply answers work already under way, so a document written from it would start that work a second time. Or one collapsed line per repository could count those folders, with nothing to do about them.

Why this is proposed

The 6 repositories checked hold 15 source-material folders, all committed: 2 hold a brief or an intake record and already have their documents written, so neither is listed, and of the other 13 only 1, an unfinished intake, is one step from ready. The brief, agreed 2026-11-23, puts under Not ready yet “a folder under source-material/ holding neither a brief nor an intake record”; it was approved through screens that never showed what real repositories hold. The request, 2026-11-23, asked that the kinds of source material be “distinct formal things”, without which it was unclear “how we would support that kind of UI”. An unfinished intake is one of them; a stakeholder’s reply and a handoff package are not, and a folder’s name can’t tell a reply from a handoff.

02 / SECTION

Where Kiln stops for you, and starting the build

Kiln stops for you at two points: the early review, once the requirements document is refined and before any design work, and the final review, once the requirements are finished and before the build. At each it opens a stakeholder review page like this one, and the final review also shows the phase plan the build will follow.

Key acceptance criteria & mockups

  • When the method made no stakeholder review at a stop, Kiln has one made, so there is always a page to read. Source
  • You answer by sending feedback, continuing without any, or working in your own session and pressing Resume. Source
  • After one round of feedback at the early review, Kiln carries on to the design without waiting, unless you ask it to stop again. Source
  • The wait at the early review is on by default; you can turn it off before Start or at any point until refinement finishes, and the review is still made. Source
  • The final review, the phase plan and Start the build share one screen, so there is no screen that only says continue. Source
  • Starting the build is how you say the review is done: it goes ahead on any assumption still unconfirmed, and the screen says how many. Source
  • Kiln builds only from a phase plan: if the requirements finish without one, Start the build is unavailable until you write it in your own session and press Resume. Source

03 / SECTION

Before Start

Choosing an item opens a screen showing what Kiln found and the requirements plan: the stages Kiln intends to run, in order, read from the Enso Method installed on your computer, followed by the build. Nothing works on the document until you press Start.

Key acceptance criteria & mockups

  • Kiln reads the requirements plan in a short agent session as soon as the home screen opens or kiln run starts, before Start, and reuses it until the method changes. Source
  • Start never waits for the requirements plan; if it can’t be read, Start still works and the plan fills in as stages run. Source
  • On a pay-per-use route, the billing approval you give before Start also covers reading the plan and every session that applies feedback. Source · 2
  • One feature branch, cut when the first stage starts and named after the source folder, carries the requirements and the build to a single pull request. Source
  • Kiln pushes that branch after every stage, so draft requirements are on the remote repository within minutes. Source
  • Work whose refinement or feedback round is part-way through, with changes not committed, is refused until the session doing that round finishes it or is stopped. Source

What should work or look differently in this section?

04 / SECTION

While it runs: progress and feedback

Each stage runs in a fresh agent session in the feature’s own working copy, with the controls a build phase has today: Message Claude, Pause, and Needs you when a stage ends without finishing. Feedback is anything you tell Kiln about the requirements, typed or pasted from a review’s reply.

Key acceptance criteria & mockups

  • Within minutes of the draft, the running screen shows its few key statements and what it leaves out, so you can catch a wrong turn before hours of refinement. Source
  • Feedback reaches every document already written, the design and phase plan included, not only the requirements document. Source
  • If the method is updated during a run, the next stage follows the new plan; finished stages keep their record, and a notice says what changed. Source
  • If the method says the material should first become an initiative of several documents, the run halts at Needs you, where the only choice is to reset Kiln for that work. Source
  • From a terminal, kiln status shows where a document stands, and there are commands to send feedback, continue past the early review, start the build and change a stage’s model. Source · 2

What should work or look differently in this section?

05 / SECTION

Which model runs each stage

Every stage in the requirements plan shows the agent, model and effort it runs on, with Change, as each build phase does today. Model defaults is the settings page holding the model each kind of work starts on; it gains two rows, one for requirements stages and one for refining the design.

Key acceptance criteria & mockups

  • Requirements stages default to Claude Code with Fable at high effort, falling back to Codex with GPT Astra at high. Source
  • Refining the design, the longest stage, defaults to the next model down in capability, Opus at high effort, falling back to GPT Sol at extra high. Source
  • A model chosen for one stage can be remembered for that stage on all future work. Source
  • If the method renames or replaces that stage, the remembered choice stops applying and the stage says so, rather than carrying it over. Source
  • A model that can’t be used stops the run, and nothing runs in its place; the fallback applies only to a stage not yet started. Source

HOME-001Confidence: 85%Impact: MediumNo reply needed

Should work Kiln can’t tell is built or unfinished go in one collapsed list at the end of the home screen?

Yes. Documents with no phase plan, no Kiln run, no refinement under way and no unmerged branch go in one collapsed line at the end, which says Kiln can’t tell whether they were built or left unfinished.

Details and optional reply

A small document built by hand in one session looks the same as one left unfinished. Opened, the line lists them newest change first, and each opens like work under way. Work Kiln took to its final review never lands here, and once the method writes a phase document for everything it builds, work built by hand after that shows as built, so the group holds work left unfinished and work built before that change.

If you choose otherwise: Left off the home screen, work started by hand on the shared branch could be opened only by typing the kiln run command. Listed with the work under way, Kiln’s own repository would open on nine lines that need nothing.

9 of the 28 requirement folders in Kiln’s own repository have no phase plan, and all nine are built. Only their commit wording shows it, and the brief rules out Kiln reading that wording, since the method may reword its commits. Without it, Git can’t tell built work from unfinished work when only documents changed, which was true of 4 finished pieces of work in other repositories checked. From the request, 2026-11-23: “reviewing it is a real tax for humans”, which argues against lines that need nothing; and of work started by hand, “Wherever it picks up, it just knows where you left off”, which argues against hiding it.
